societies.name: Star Trek — The Ba’ku’s chosen handwork
societies.society: Technically capable village deliberately avoiding daily labor-saving machines

scope.period: The established village before the attempted forced relocation
scope.population: Living Ba’ku villagers, explicitly a humanoid alien population analogy
exclusions: Natural rejuvenation as a production machine
A detailed communal property/benefits system not established by the film

societies.description:
The Ba’ku know advanced technology but deliberately avoid using it in everyday life. Sojef explicitly connects this choice with preserving the value of a person’s own work when machines could do it instead. This gives a direct zero-variant rationale grounded in an actual technological alternative and a stated social choice. The planet’s rejuvenating environment is separate: long life is not the productive automation mechanism.

The available short references do not establish how food, housing and care are guaranteed, or who finally owns village productive resources, so those coordinates remain unresolved. A shared-community analogy is only a provisional regime comparison, not a claim of equal ownership. The village can exile dissidents, and external relocation threatens its way of life; peaceful appearances are not an unconditional rights charter. Ba’ku are explicitly treated as humanoid aliens for the human-oriented axes. Farming, craft, teaching and care remain useful work, and the selected rejection of labor-saving machines does not establish an all-age nonworking percentage.

guarantees.basis: The film dialogue explicitly chooses retained humanlike work over labor-saving machines, but ordinary guarantee institutions are not specified.

control.basis: Village property and final productive authority are not established; the shared-community regime analogy remains provisional.

nonworking.basis: Ba’ku are a disclosed humanoid alien proxy. Actual handwork, teaching and care continue and no all-age participation census is supplied.

evidence.locator: Bounded named-society economic and story sections

societies.name: Red Dwarf — The early survivor household
societies.society: Long-term machine-supported life aboard the original ship after Lister awakens

scope.continuity: Television series I–II aboard Red Dwarf; no novel continuity
scope.period: Established post-awakening ship life, excluding the temporary Queeg access restriction
scope.population: Living Dave Lister and active human-derived holographic Arnold Rimmer, a disclosed tiny population proxy
exclusions: Dead crew and Lister’s earlier stasis as active leisure
Feline-derived Cat or original machine minds as humans
Starbug, revived crew, later alternate Kochanski and later ship states
Stored input stocks as infinite fabrication

societies.description:
After Lister awakens, the ship’s automated service network continues supplying daily food, drink and habitat support without an ordinary outside wage economy. Dispensers process and deliver from large cargo and stasis stores rather than creating unlimited matter. Rimmer’s active holographic life is also sustained by the computer. The favorable guarantee estimate applies to this tiny continuing household, qualified by equipment faults, stored-input limits and permission-dependent access.

Holly operates the sustaining ship systems, while individual dispensers also have independent AI. Human requests do not establish final ownership; the computer’s Queeg prank demonstrates that access can temporarily be withheld. Control consequently leans toward autonomous machine provision, with uncertainty about human clearances and inherited company rules. Lister is living, and active human-derived Rimmer is the explicit posthuman proxy; Cat, machine minds and dead crew are excluded. Repair, navigation, problem-solving and care remain useful activities. Their small number and frequent leisure cannot be converted into a population nonworking percentage or confused with time spent resting.

guarantees.basis: Automated stored-input services and computer-maintained habitation/holography support actual continuing residents, qualified by permissions, faults and finite stocks.

control.basis: Holly and independent dispenser AIs retain operational/access power; Queeg is Holly’s temporary prank, not a separate sovereign or society.

nonworking.basis: Only living Lister and active human-derived Rimmer form the disclosed tiny proxy. Useful technical and care activity continues; leisure time is not a population fraction.

societies.name: Sufficiently Advanced — Stardweller basics

scope.continuity: First-edition Stardweller civilization; later alternate-setting catch-all excluded
scope.population: Living humans and active human-derived Stardweller persons
exclusions: Social lack of recognition as automatic loss of food

societies.description:
First-edition Stardweller society makes the basics of life available to everyone and organizes its economy to reduce material inequality. Replicator and transmutation technology supplies the productive context. Peer recognition matters strongly, but the economic passage explicitly distinguishes social and emotional frustration from material deprivation. Guarantees therefore receive a strong favorable estimate, with ordinary resource conditions and the limited excerpt preventing a perfect entitlement claim.

The short gathered passages do not establish who holds final productive ownership and override authority throughout this diverse civilization. Control remains unresolved rather than equating an equalizing economy with complete distributed human ownership or treating advanced digital residents as an AI state. The guaranteed-provider regime is provisional, with a distributed alternative left open. Humans and active human-derived persons are an explicit proxy within a broader population. Science, design, teaching, care and esteem-seeking contributions remain useful work. Secure basics and a preference for recognition over money do not determine how many people perform none of those activities.

guarantees.basis: The first-edition passage explicitly ensures basics for everyone within the replicator/transmutation economy and distinguishes esteem problems from material poverty.

control.basis: Equalization and advanced citizens do not establish final ownership/override institutions; neither shared human control nor machine sovereignty is assumed numerically.

nonworking.basis: Useful science, design, teaching and care continue; active human-derived persons are a disclosed proxy and no all-person work census is given.
